definition:
In the Bible wisdom is not mainly cleverness or a store of information. It is skill in living well in God's world: knowing how things are made to work, reading people and situations truly, choosing the right word at the right time, and ordering a life toward what is good. Its root is religious, not technical. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), and “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10), which means that wisdom starts with reverent trust in the God who made the world and set its order. Proverbs teaches how life generally goes for the diligent and the lazy, the honest and the deceitful; Job and Ecclesiastes test those patterns against suffering, injustice, and death; and the New Testament presents Jesus Christ as “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The fear of the LORD, Scripture's name for the reverent awe that underlies wisdom, has its own study.

The main Hebrew noun is ḥokmâ, with the adjective ḥākām, ‘wise’. Its range shows its practical cast: it can describe the skill of craftsmen who made the tabernacle (Exodus 28:3; 31:3), the shrewdness of a counselor, the justice of a good king, and the moral insight of the godly. Alongside it stand bînâ and tĕbûnâ (‘understanding’, ‘discernment’), daʿat (‘knowledge’, including personal acquaintance), mûsār (‘discipline’ or ‘instruction’, often including correction), and ʿormâ (‘prudence’, ‘shrewdness’). Proverbs names several kinds of fool: the petî, the ‘simple’ or naive person who can still learn; the kĕsîl and ʾĕwîl, the dull and the stubborn fool; the lēṣ, the ‘mocker’ who scorns correction; and the nābāl, whose folly is moral and godless (Psalm 14:1). A proverb is a māšāl, a short comparison or saying. In Greek, sophia and sophos translate the Hebrew family, with phronēsis (‘practical good sense’) and synesis (‘understanding’); the opposite is mōria, ‘foolishness’, the word Paul uses when he calls the message of the cross foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:18).
ot:
Wisdom first appears in Scripture as something reached for wrongly. The woman in Eden saw that the forbidden tree was “desirable for obtaining wisdom” (Genesis 3:6), and the story turns on the attempt to know good and evil on human terms, apart from God's word. From then on the Bible distinguishes wisdom received from God from wisdom seized against him. Joseph is recognized by Pharaoh as “discerning and wise” (Genesis 41:39) because God reveals to him the meaning of dreams, and the craftsmen of the tabernacle are filled with God's Spirit and with skill for their work (Exodus 31:3). Moses tells Israel that keeping God's statutes will itself be their wisdom before the nations, who will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people” (Deuteronomy 4:6). Wisdom in the Old Testament is never merely secular technique, and never merely religious feeling; it reaches from the workshop to the law court to worship.

Solomon is the Old Testament's model of the wise king. Given the choice of any gift, he asked for “an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9), and God gave him wisdom, riches, and honor. His judgment between the two mothers (1 Kings 3:16-28) shows wisdom in the service of justice. The narrator says Solomon's wisdom exceeded that of the East and of Egypt, that he spoke thousands of proverbs and songs, and that he taught about trees, animals, birds, and fish (1 Kings 4:29-34). The comparison is instructive: Israel knew that other nations had wisdom traditions, and archaeology has recovered many of them, including Egyptian instructions of a father to a son and Mesopotamian proverb collections. Most scholars since Adolf Erman's study of 1924 have recognized a close relationship between Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22 and the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. Israel's sages learned from their neighbors while setting everything they learned under the fear of the LORD. Yet Solomon's own story is a warning: the wisest of kings ended by turning his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:1-13). Wisdom as a gift does not guarantee wisdom as a life.

The book of Proverbs, attributed in its headings to Solomon and to other sages (Agur and Lemuel in chapters 30 and 31, and ‘the men of Hezekiah’ who copied a collection in 25:1), gives the canon its fullest school of wisdom. Chapters 1 to 9 are a father's appeals to a son, set between two women: Lady Wisdom, who calls in the streets and builds her house, and the adulteress or Woman Folly, whose house leads to death. The poem of Proverbs 8 presents Wisdom as present with God before creation: “The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old” (Proverbs 8:22), and at his side “a skilled craftsman” and “His delight day by day” (Proverbs 8:30). The Hebrew verb in 8:22, qānâ, usually means ‘to acquire’ and sometimes ‘to create’; the Greek Septuagint rendered it ‘created’, the Latin Vulgate ‘possessed’, and English translations still divide. The word ʾāmôn in 8:30 is also disputed: ‘craftsman’, or ‘little child’, or ‘faithfully’. The point of the poem is clear either way: “The LORD founded the earth by wisdom” (Proverbs 3:19), so the world has an order that can be learned, and wisdom is the way to live in step with it. The collections of sayings that follow (chapters 10 to 29) teach how life usually goes: diligence tends toward plenty, laziness toward want, honesty toward trust, and violence toward ruin. They are observations and counsel, not guarantees, and the book itself shows that they must be applied with judgment: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” stands directly beside “Answer a fool according to his folly” (Proverbs 26:4-5). The Talmud records that some sages once considered withdrawing Proverbs because of apparent contradictions like this, and resolved them by distinguishing different situations, which is exactly the skill the book is training. It ends with a portrait of a valiant woman whose life of work, generosity, and fear of the LORD embodies Lady Wisdom (Proverbs 31:10-31).

Job and Ecclesiastes press on the limits of that pattern. Job is righteous and suffers catastrophe, and his friends, arguing that suffering must be punishment for sin, turn true observations into false verdicts. Job 28 asks where wisdom can be found and answers that humans can mine the earth for gold but cannot dig out wisdom; only God knows its place, and to humanity he says, “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28). When God finally answers Job out of the whirlwind, he gives no explanation of Job's suffering but a tour of creation's wonders that Job cannot comprehend (Job 38 to 41), and then declares that Job, not his friends, has spoken rightly (Job 42:7). Ecclesiastes, spoken by Qohelet (‘the Teacher’, perhaps ‘one who gathers an assembly’), tests every road to meaning under the sun and calls each hebel, a word meaning ‘breath’ or ‘vapor’ that the BSB renders “futility” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The wise and the fool both die; “time and chance happen to all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11); no one can find out the whole work of God (Ecclesiastes 8:17). Yet the book repeatedly commends receiving food, work, and love as God's gift, and ends by calling its reader to “Fear God and keep His commandments” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Together these books teach that wisdom includes knowing what one cannot know.

Wisdom runs through the rest of the Old Testament too. Psalms 1, 37, 49, 73, and 112 are often called wisdom psalms, and Psalm 90 prays, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). The prophets condemn the wisdom of those who are wise in their own eyes (Isaiah 5:21; 29:14) and command, “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom” (Jeremiah 9:23), but to boast in knowing the LORD. Isaiah promises a king from Jesse's line on whom will rest “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:2). Daniel confesses that “wisdom and power belong to Him” (Daniel 2:20). In the centuries before Christ, Jewish writings kept developing the theme: Sirach (Ben Sira, about 180 BC) identified wisdom with the law of Moses (Sirach 24), and the Wisdom of Solomon (usually dated between the first century BC and the early first century AD) described wisdom as a reflection of God's eternal light. These books, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in their Old Testament and Protestants read as Apocrypha, form part of the background of the New Testament's language about Christ.
nt:
The Gospels present Jesus as wise from childhood; Luke says that he “grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52), and his hometown asked where he got such wisdom (Mark 6:2). He taught like a sage, in parables, proverbs, and riddles, and ended the Sermon on the Mount with a wisdom contrast between two builders: everyone who hears his words and does them “is like a wise man who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24). But he claimed more than a sage could. He said that the Queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, “and now One greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). He said that “wisdom is vindicated by her actions” (Matthew 11:19), speaking of his own ministry, and where Luke's Gospel introduces a saying with “the wisdom of God said” (Luke 11:49), Matthew's parallel has Jesus say in his own person, “I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers” (Matthew 23:34). His invitation, “Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me” (Matthew 11:29), echoes the language Jewish wisdom writing used for taking on wisdom's yoke (as in Sirach 51:26). And he thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and learned and revealing them to little children (Matthew 11:25): the wisdom he brought overturns human estimates of who is wise.

John's prologue speaks of the Word who was with God in the beginning and through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3), language that many interpreters hear as an echo of Wisdom beside God at creation in Proverbs 8, as well as of Genesis 1. Paul makes the identification explicit and sharpens it. To Corinthian believers who prized eloquence and knowledge, he wrote that “the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18). God chose to save through what the world thought foolish, a crucified Messiah, so that “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) is known in the place of weakness, and so that no one may boast before him. Christ “has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). This is not a rejection of thinking. Paul says that among the mature he does speak wisdom, “the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 2:7), which the rulers of this age did not understand, “For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8), and which the Spirit reveals.

The later letters apply the same confession to creation and to daily life. Colossians calls the Son “the image of the invisible God” through whom and for whom all things were created and in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:15-17), the role Proverbs gave to Wisdom, and says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). Hebrews calls the Son “the radiance of God's glory” (Hebrews 1:3), using a rare Greek word, apaugasma, that also appears in the Wisdom of Solomon's description of wisdom (7:26). Ephesians speaks of God's “manifold wisdom” displayed through the church (Ephesians 3:10) and tells believers to walk “not as unwise but as wise” (Ephesians 5:15). Paul breaks into doxology at the depth of God's wisdom, whose ways are beyond tracing (Romans 11:33). James is the New Testament's wisdom book. He promises that anyone who lacks wisdom “should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault” (James 1:5), and contrasts earthly wisdom, marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, with “the wisdom from above,” which is “pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit” (James 3:17). Wisdom here is known by its fruit in conduct. In Revelation the heavenly chorus ascribes wisdom to the slain Lamb (Revelation 5:12): the one the world judged foolish is the wisdom by which the world was made.

keyTexts.why: The first grasp at wisdom is made against God's word. The Bible's contrast between received wisdom and seized wisdom begins here.
Keeping God's statutes is Israel's wisdom before the nations. Wisdom and law are not rivals.
Solomon asks for an understanding heart to govern justly, and his judgment between two mothers shows wisdom in the service of justice.
The purpose of Proverbs and its motto: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.
Wisdom present with God before and at creation, a poem the New Testament and the church read in the light of Christ.
Two opposite sayings side by side, showing that proverbs require judgment about which fits the case.
Humans can mine the earth but cannot find wisdom; only God knows its place, and he gives it as the fear of the Lord.
The book's epilogue commends the Teacher's words and sums up the matter: fear God and keep his commandments.
The coming king from Jesse's line will be endowed with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding.
Wisdom hidden from the wise and revealed to little children, and Jesus' invitation to take his yoke.
The cross is foolishness to the world and the wisdom of God. Christ has become our wisdom.
All things were created through and for the Son and hold together in him, the role Proverbs gave to Wisdom.
In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
The wisdom from above is known by its fruit: purity, peace, gentleness, mercy, and sincerity.

history:
Jewish readers wrestled with the wisdom books before Christians did. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records a dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel over whether Ecclesiastes belonged among the holy writings, and the Talmud (Shabbat 30b) tells of sages who considered withdrawing Proverbs and Ecclesiastes over apparent contradictions before resolving them. Early Christian writers read Proverbs 8 as speaking of the Son. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho (mid second century), used it to argue that a divine person was with the Father before creation. That reading became the battleground of the Arian controversy in the fourth century. Arius and his supporters argued from the Greek ‘created’ in Proverbs 8:22 that the Son was the first and highest creature. Athanasius answered, in his Orations against the Arians, that the verse refers to the Son's taking of created human nature for the sake of redemption, not to his eternal being, and the Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son ‘begotten, not made’. The emperor Justinian's great church in Constantinople, dedicated in 537, was named Hagia Sophia, ‘Holy Wisdom’, in honor of Christ the Word.

Augustine distinguished two kinds of knowing in On the Trinity (books 12 to 14): scientia, knowledge of temporal things used well, and sapientia, the contemplation of eternal things, fulfilled in knowing God. Gregory the Great's Moralia on Job (late sixth century) made that book a school of moral and spiritual formation for medieval readers. Thomas Aquinas treated wisdom both as an intellectual virtue and as a gift of the Holy Spirit (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 45), following the medieval list of seven gifts drawn from Isaiah 11:2-3 in its Greek and Latin form, which adds ‘piety’ to the six gifts of the Hebrew. John Calvin opened his Institutes (1.1.1) by saying that nearly all true wisdom consists of two parts, the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves, and that the two are bound together. The Puritans prized practical ‘wisdom for living’, and the churches kept reading Proverbs as instruction for the young.

Modern scholarship has reshaped how the wisdom books are read. The discovery and publication of Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom texts showed how much Israel's sages shared with their neighbors, and Adolf Erman's comparison of Proverbs with the Instruction of Amenemope (1924) became a standard example. Walther Zimmerli argued in 1964 that wisdom thinks within a theology of creation rather than of Israel's saving history, and Gerhard von Rad's Wisdom in Israel (German edition 1970) described wisdom as Israel's way of trusting God's order in the world while respecting its limits. More recent scholars have stressed wisdom's ties to covenant and to Israel's worship. In Russian Orthodox thought the ‘sophiology’ of Sergius Bulgakov, which developed Wisdom as a principle linking God and creation, was condemned in 1935 by the Moscow Patriarchate and by the Russian Church Outside Russia, while others defended it, and it remains debated. Across traditions the church confesses that Christ is the Wisdom of God, and that human wisdom is received as a gift, not achieved as a possession.

differ.view: Proverbs 8 as a portrait of the Son
differ.body: Many church fathers, and many later readers, took the Wisdom of Proverbs 8 as the eternal Son speaking before his incarnation. The New Testament attributes Wisdom's roles to Christ: he is with God in the beginning, all things are made through him, and all things hold together in him (John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17). Justin Martyr and Athanasius read the chapter this way, differing only on how to take ‘created’ in verse 22, and defenders today argue that the New Testament authorizes reading the passage directly of Christ, provided the verse is not taken to make the Son a creature.

differ.view: Proverbs 8 as a personification fulfilled in Christ
differ.body: Other interpreters, including many modern Old Testament scholars across traditions, read Lady Wisdom in Proverbs 1 to 9 as a vivid poetic personification of God's own wisdom, set opposite the personified Woman Folly. On this view the poem's first meaning is that creation has an order God designed and that wisdom is older than human cleverness. The New Testament then draws on this figure to say who Christ is, so that Proverbs 8 is fulfilled in him by typology and theme rather than read as a direct description of the Son. Defenders note that the book's own frame is the father's instruction to a son about ordinary life, and that the Nicene faith does not depend on this chapter.

The Teacher of Ecclesiastes is a wise and orthodox guide who strips away false hopes so that his readers can receive life as God's gift. His repeated counsel to eat, drink, work, and find joy (Ecclesiastes 2:24-26; 5:18-20; 9:7-10) is not despair but faith within the limits of a fallen world, and his refrain of hebel names life's brevity and elusiveness rather than its meaninglessness. R. N. Whybray argued this line in an influential 1982 article presenting Qohelet as a preacher of joy, and many readers, ancient and modern, hear the book as sober wisdom that the epilogue commends.

differ.view: Qohelet's voice weighed by the frame
differ.body: Other scholars, including Michael V. Fox and Tremper Longman III, stress that the book presents Qohelet's words through a narrator who speaks of him in the third person (Ecclesiastes 1:1-2; 7:27; 12:8-14). Qohelet's search under the sun reaches genuinely troubling conclusions, and the narrator's epilogue sets them within the fear of God and coming judgment. On this reading, the book teaches by letting a searching and often pessimistic voice be heard in full and then showing where wisdom must stand. Readers holding this view see the book as an honest map of life without the larger horizon that the rest of Scripture supplies.

errors:
The church has rejected the idea that wisdom is secret knowledge reserved for an elite. The Gnostic systems of the second century, answered by Irenaeus of Lyon in Against Heresies (about 180), spun myths in which a divine being named Sophia fell and knowledge of that myth brought salvation. Scripture's wisdom is public, practical, and moral, open to the simple who will learn, and its fullest form is a crucified Messiah proclaimed openly. The church also rejected the Arian use of Proverbs 8:22 to make the Son a creature, confessing at Nicaea that he is begotten, not made, and of one being with the Father. A third distortion turns Proverbs into a contract: do these things and you will surely be healthy and rich. That was the mistake of Job's friends, and God said they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7).

Two opposite errors recur. One is contempt for learning, as if faith needed no thought and every human insight outside Scripture were worthless. The Bible's own sages learned from other nations, Solomon studied plants and animals, and the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, not its end. The other is confidence in human wisdom as self-sufficient, whether ancient philosophy or modern expertise, measured by its own standards and closed to God. Paul's word to Corinth stands against both: God has made foolish the wisdom of the world, and yet Christ has become for believers the wisdom from God.
life:
Biblical wisdom is learned slowly and mostly in ordinary places: at work, in the family, with money, in speech, in friendships. Proverbs trains attention to small daily choices (how one answers, spends, listens, and works) because character is built there. It also trains humility: the wise person listens to advice, accepts correction, and knows that plans must be held loosely before God (Proverbs 16:9). A person seeking wisdom can start where James does, by asking God, who gives generously, and by keeping company with the wise, since the one who walks with the wise grows wise (Proverbs 13:20).

The whole canon's wisdom also guards against cruelty. Because the pattern of Proverbs is general and not mechanical, a Christian may not look at someone's illness, poverty, or grief and conclude that it must be their fault; Job's friends did that and were rebuked. Ecclesiastes gives permission to admit that much of life cannot be explained and to receive daily gifts with gratitude anyway. And because Christ is the wisdom of God, the measure of a wise life is finally not success but likeness to the one who was gentle and humble in heart and who chose the cross.
questions: Proverbs 26:4-5 gives two opposite pieces of advice side by side. What does that teach about how proverbs are meant to be used, and where have you seen a true saying misapplied?
Job's friends said many true things and still spoke wrongly about God. What made their wisdom fail, and how can a person comfort a sufferer without repeating their mistake?
Paul calls the crucified Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). How does the cross challenge the ways your own culture defines wisdom and success?
